Hands-down, my FAVORITE spin-off installment to a main series I have ever played. I had low expectations, my bad. I was more or less assuming this would be a lot more spin-offy, a la full of gimmicks, over-reliance of fanservice, snide jibes at the main game, tryhard attempts to assert superiority over its source material and failing while still riding hard on the main titles to gain any traction, etc. etc.

What I played instead was an astonishingly well-executed storyline that fits cohesively into the primary plot of of the series. It still very much feels like a Danganronpa game, but has a stand-out unique charm all its own. This spin-off is officially my favorite game in the Danganronpa series.

This is exactly how a spin-off should be handled more often: as its own wholly developed arc that still deepens and clarifies elements of the established world, rather than convolutes (@KingdomHearts). Rather than running in parallel to the main story, this game readily intertwines with multiple tie-ins.

Ultra Despair Girls can be seen as an inversion of the rest of the series. Whereas Danganronpa otherwise places 'Ultimate' people in point-and-click gameplay that exposits exclusively via heavy text dialogue, this game places a completely Normal girl in an extreme and wild situation immersed in action. (Think a watered down Left4Dead with a some simple puzzles, and a lot more character narrative thrown in.)

Throughout the story, it's expressed repeatedly that Komaru isn't the hero because she was born special or with any inherent talent that boosts her chances of survival; instead, her agency develops organically through the choices she makes.

This falls right in line with Danganronpa's previous protagnists who are rather unremarkable in contrast to the supporting cast of stand-out characters with outlandish backstories, and emphasizes further the point that being normal isn't bad and doesn't necessarily render a person incapable-- normal people still do amazing things.

In foil to Komaru, Toko absolutely shined in this game. She was way too good a character to have been quickly done-away with after the first game ended, and it was incredibly entertaining to see Ultra Despair Girls properly drag her out into the foreground and utilize her in full Toko-essence. Much of the comic relief blooms from Toko's total awkward weirdness and odd tangents.

The dynamic between the two highly contrasted girls was a treat in every small interaction, and the development of their friendship felt entirely true-to-character and like a natural progression. Watching Toko flounder and Komaru tiptoe around each other gives ALL the warm and fuzzies-- an act that played remarkably well against the backdrop of gore, horrific implications, and psychological thrills. And yes, this game goes HARD with the latter.

With the villains being a group of small children who go on a murder spree, any kind of happy backstory was NOT to be expected in the slightest, right? But the fact that these are kids just twists the knife even deeper, and deeper still as you play the game and continue to uncover all the gutwrenching facets of the plotline. All of this eased in balance with the levity of typical Danganronpa antics and weird segues to keep throwing you for a loop.

That said about the writing-- both english VAs for Komaru and Toko blew brought their a-game in delivery, which did even more for overall enjoyability. And listen, I'm TeamSubs more often than not, so suffice to say I was pleasantly surprised with the english audio.

Gameplay feels a bit rough at times, which can be frustrating if you're a precision player. But if you're just looking for a game to breeze through and have a hell of a time doing so, Ultra Despair Girls is definitely not a waste.

Edit: I just wanted to update this review with a quick TLDR after playing quite a bit more Fallout4 VR.

[b]TLDR:[/b] I have 300+ games in my account, and have played thousands of hours of video games, and Fallout 4 VR is the best video game experience of my life. It's not just a video game. You are there.

I actually couldn't really get into Fallout 4 (normal screen), but in VR it's obviously totally different. The immersion is great, and the performance and graphics and so on are all fine for me (note that I did not start actually playing until June 2018, so I am not familiar with the release issues, even though I bought it awhile ago). This and Skyrim are basically the killer apps for VR. Locomotion and VR feel in both are great and I get no nausea.

I use the Samsung Odyssey, 6700k and gtx1070, runs well and I have some mods installed. Vortex and that INI editor are easy to use. I use darker nights, easy hacking, craftable ammo, FAR, Vivid Fallout, Improved reflex sights, and more accurate weapons, basically just stuff to improve the vanilla experience a bit. Inventory use takes some practice in VR, and is boring to me in and out of VR, so I just used console commands to set the carry weight to effectively infinite.

one thing I'd like to note as well is that if you have the common criticism of Fallout games that, innately because of the setting, they are a bit ugly to walk around (this actually prevented me from enjoying the flatscreen version) I find that it's much better in VR. You can appreciate all the little details and bits of color and here and there, rather than feeling like you are walking over the same brown/grey rubble and dirt everywhere. The horror bits can also be genuinely scary.

I never had the DLCs so I can't really address the controversy or dismay over those not being added. The fact that they can be modded in pretty easily means it probably wasn't a technical challenge that kept them out, but some kind of business/publishing issue. the DLCs are included in SkyrimVR, probably because it's much older and they don't expect to sell them anymore on the flat screen version. It could even be contractual. I dunno, there's already way more content in vanilla Fallout4 than you are going to end up playing in VR anyway, just because of the limitations on VR playtime. I mean, you could play it all, but VR tends to be done in relatively short sessions for a variety of reasons.

If you already exhausted the content in Fallout 4 flat screen you might find yourself unwilling to go through it again just for the sake of the VR experience. Depends on whether you are the sort of person who plays video games more than once. I'm not really, so it was a bit hard for me to play a lot of SkyrimVR beyond the couple of things I hadn't already tried, because I played vanilla so much. BUT, as discussed I didn't play much Fallout 4 flatscreen (only about 90 minutes actually) so this is all new to me, and I'm going to play it a lot. If you haven't played them yet, then Fallout 4 VR and Skyrim VR are the best VR, and maybe gaming period, experiences you can have. Yeah, you can quibble all day over little shortcomings here and there, but at the end of the day you are walking around The Commonwealth like you are really there, and in comparison to that all of the little complaints kind of fade away.

It has been a long time since I played a game, maybe even watched a film that captivated me as much as Cognition did. If like myself you're a fan of detective games then this is a must. I can't even compare any other games that match it in terms of how well thought out the story is. The twists, murders, story/skills development and style flow seamlessly from episode to episode. This is how episodic games should be done, full stop. The suspense and cliff hangers at the end of each episode have subtly been built up from the beginning of each ep, they're not just thrown at you in the last 5 minutes in hopes to keep you invested long enough to buy the next one.   

The use of the cognition skill works really well in the game. You do equal amounts of normal detective work with a nice topping of physic abilities. You don't feel as Erica is over powered in anyway, even without the powers she makes a kick ass detective. With some top quality voice acting going on I might add.  

The puzzles are original and unique the majority of times. So you don't run the chance of becoming immune to them, you can't just jump head first into them because there's a good chance you could get yourself killed. They're not gonna hold your hand either, there's a level of effort you got to put in.

So negative point, I found the animations to be a bit jerky, and it would take Erica nearly 10 seconds to register how to  turn around and walk across the room. I don't know whether this was because I played most of the game on the "Fastest" setting (cause's some hilarious glitches in the character model) but for the last ep I did change the settings to beautiful and most of what I just mentioned above disappeared. So do yourself a favour and don't play on the fastest settings; your computer can handle it at peak quality! I was just an idiot. 

End mark, I give it a 9.5 out of 10. It's orginal, well made and worth every penny.

Insurgency is one hell of a beast, created by mixing up all the good things from other great FPS title.
It has the realism of Red Orchestra / Rising Storm that adds a great immersion and intense atmosphere, the small skimrish maps akin to Counter  Strike for a quick and fun close quarter battles, great weapon customization system that reminds me to Rainbow Six / Ghost  Recon, and Battlefield's class based gameplay. 

Looks unoriginal eh? Nah, not at all. Insurgency DO feels like a combination, something "in between" of those game, but the devs executed the ideas impressively that I can consider Insurgency as an original, somewhat one of a kind game that still maintain its own unique identity among an ocean of FPSes nowadays.

Gameplay (10/10)
Immersive, intense, hardcore, yet it still can offer a fun and enjoyable experience. Insurgency is one of those "easy  to learn hard to master" game. Naturally, Insurgency itself is a very simple game, the thing that you'll have to learn is how the general system works, weapons and attachments, the different set of classes, and the realism factor itself. I believe you'll fully understand how the game works in around an hour, or even less. Insurgency isn't for a trigger-happy FPS player. Patience, teamwork, and careful observation of your surrounding is the key here. Even if you already do that, like walking slowly, crouch, peeking on corners, you'll find yourself in  "WHERE THE FUCK IS THE BULLET COME FROM?" situation, first shot, screen blurred, second shot, you started to panic, third shot and you're dead. In many occassion you don't even have the time to be panicked, you'll have an instant death. 

Another great aspect of this game is how devs design the overall system. No grinding, no perk, just pure skill and tactic. Shitload of varied game modes that actually..well..varied, a balanced class system. Overall Insurgency is, one of the most balanced and fair FPS I've ever played.

Sound (10/10)
I could've put it in the gameplay section, since the sound isn't just to make the game more atmospheric, but the sound design is a part of the gameplay, its a crucial part. For a modern military FPS with a flare of relism, the sound must be designed to make the game, not only immersive and realitic, but also "usable" and its actually a part of the tactic. Yes, the sound is mind-blowingly fantastic. I love how detailed the sounds are, the sound of bullets blazing over your head, hitting the wall or floor, fly near your ears, and when it do hit you, everything become muffed. The guns sounds realistic, it doesn't sound too weak, yet doesn't sound THAT powerful.  Sound is your best friend and your greatest enemy.

Graphic (9/10)
Insurgency is built from Source Engine, which is, in a way..dated. But. thanks for the great level design and visual effect, and of course the gameplay. You'll find Insurgency's graphic to be a brilliant one. You might think Battlefield has the most realistic graphic for a FPS game. That might be true, but Battlefield's graphic is just too beautiful to be realistc, I find it more in the cinematic side. Insurgency, in the other side can capture the overall atmosphere of a battlefield. A battlefield is supposed to be "ugly", no filtering, no lens flare, it's rough. No, no.. I don't say Insurgency graphic is  ugly, far from it. It's a bit dated yes, but the "dated" factor and the genius devs behind the game make Insurgency's graphic looks truly believable. 

Conclusion (10/10)
Immersive, believeable, realistic, hardcore, tactical, yet still fun, enjoyable, and pretty much accesible. Insurgency is a perfect balance of realistc / hardcore FPS game with the close quarter combat fun and quick matches of a more arcade-ish FPS game. Insurgency does take inspiration from a wide range of FPS game type, but the devs cleverly managed to distinguish the game to something more unique that can stand at its own two feet and overall maintaining its own identity of a new kind of FPS game.

Undertale is a rather disappointing game, especially as it is so highly acclaimed by everyone I have spoken to about it and it is all over the internet.

I found that the game became very repetitive and quite dull after a small amount of time, as I thought story wasn't very enticing; mainly because all of the main characters lacked originality, some of them were practically exact copies of characters from other games and others were very similar to other characters in the same story.

I also thought that the attempted 8-Bit graphics could have been a bit more refined, though this isn't a major issue, it does bother me that the game could have easily been done with more detail. However a more irritating graphical issue occurs with the playable character, as it doesn’t have any frames for diagonal movement which makes walking look slightly strange as it only has a total of eight frames for movement instead of sixteen, which would look a lot smoother and generally better, also the colour used for its hair doesn't blend in very well with background objects for most of the stages, this could've been avoided if a dark outline was used or if the hair was shaded with multiple shades of the same colour. Also, there are some sprites which are completely different from all the rest in the game, as they are much more realistic use a lot more pixels than all the others. I find that they break away from the game's style and ruin the classic look that I expect they were going for. 

Undertale also focuses too heavily on breaking the fourth wall, this is evident through all the messages when you reload saves (or even restart the game) from characters that you just spoke to before, referencing you instead of Frisk, and characters in the game actually knowing what saving is. I don't like this idea, as I find that it makes the game so much less immersive and less interesting, as you know something may be different if you reload a save, and usually when you reload a save, it because you want to restart what you just did. I find that this generally doesn't work well in games at all so this isn't just unique to Undertale.

Also, the Undertale doesn't follow many of the elements from other turn based RPG games that were successful, for example, it focuses on a world based map, with different environments for each world, going from area to area with a boss at the end of each. This kind of linear gameplay can work, but in the case of Undertale, it felt poorly thought out and if it was made up as it went along. The main issue is that each world is too short with very little enemy variety (and that you can't see the enemy you're about to fight before you fight them), and this isn't helped by the incredibly boring overworld puzzles, which are way too simple. Also, the bosses at the end of each 'stage', only feel like they're fighting you because you need to move on to the next area, not because they have an actual reason to fight you, as in many situations, they should've fought you as soon as they found you, not waited for you to walk all the way through an entire area first.

Finally, I found that Undertale's dialogue and humour was quite simplistic and childish, with silly jokes and very unappealing characters (especially as the game features a silent protagonist). Which leads on to the repetitive battle system, even though there are multiple options for taking on an opponent; I still found that battling creatures got very boring fast, as you can't really find items or a reliable upgrade system that makes battling more fun or satisfying.

In conclusion, considering this game was made by one person, it's a pretty good effort, but the flaws still outweigh the positives so I wouldn't recommend Undertale. 

I also wanted to add that everywhere I go on the internet I now see an Undertale reference, whether it be a picture of an Undertale character on someone’s avatar on a forum or the endless lists of Undertale fan art on art websites such as Deviantart; this just makes me annoyed when I see it, as I see it everywhere, however this doesn't change my opinion about the actual game, I just felt that it was necessary to mention as it is relevant to the game.

Before I go into my review let's get the Destiny comparision out of the way
After a mediocre experience with destiny that left a bad taste in my mouth, i can happily say that the Division took a smarter route for the singleplayer,multiplayer and mmo merge.

Like destiny, the Division is somewhat of a hybrite of multi and singleplayer content. The biggest difference however is "context". The area where destiny lacks the most is story and " reason" to be fighting against an enemy. The Division never has this problem. Every mission, every pickup and every sidequest have their own sence of purpose within a larger context of a wide scale biological terror attack. This helps in giving you the sence of purpose destiny so sourly lacks. It also helps in overall world building. The world is littred with small indications of what happend before and is still happening, making the user interested and invested in trying to get a grip on what is happening.

Other area's where the division wins over compatitors is the fact that world building allows for a more logical reasoning behind the streets of NY being empty. In destiny most of the world is blanc empty and a bit boring, There's little to no wildlife and everything feels pretty static.

The division isn't chock full of npc's either, but the context of the game tells us it isn;t supposed to be either. A virus killed 90% of the populatoin and the remaining few fight amongst eachother. This means that only bumbing into individuals or stray dogs and such once in a while makes perfect sence. Again world building is key and the division does a marvelous job at it.

From this point on i'll move away from my short comparison and will just focus on the game:

Coop and PVP!
The Division allows you to play alone or with friends/randoms and serves you a set of missions, encounters and sidequests to fool around in. on top of this you're pretty quickly introduced to the darkzone. The darkzone can be seen as the PVP area that also has mission content. The biggest difference with the rest of the (HUGE) world is that in the darkzone you're not save from your fellow players anymore. They can kill and loot you and o boy they will. It makes for a good mix between being able to just have fun with Coop content and PVP.

Coop in any form is done marvelously. The game has in game voicecom options and a very easy to use matchmaking/friend making system to allow you to find people to play with. There are multiple " save zones"  where you simply find other people to chill/game with by clicking on them. A nice perk right now is that the game is quite popular so you will always find someone to play with.

The graphics 
Well..if you have a nice pc..this game is beautifull. I am not sure how the game runs on lower end pc's but what I can say is that the graphics settings are very scalable. This is no mere console port, we have full support and control over what we want to turn on and off. Further more there's a good set of 3rd party support for eyetracking and such.

Gameplay
As mentioned before the story content is fun to play and the controls are easy to use, If you ever played MGS5 you'll feel right at home with this game. Basic mouse and keyboard setups work creat and I imagine that the steam controller/ xbox360 controller workout pretty nicely as well.

So is there a downside to this game?
Small bugs have been there but nothing big. 

Enemies, as mentioned in many reviews, are a bit bulletspongy. So keep in mind what type of game you are buying.

This game really is a RPG. If you want to play COD, this isn't what you'll get. Best comparision I can make is, you get MGS5/Mass effect with the skill tree and loot system of Diablo 3. Obviously the game is more than this but it should give you an idea of what you are getting in to.

all in all 9/10 in my opinion. i love the game and I am looking forward to getting back to saving NY!

Building puzzles is oddly therapeutic and Moe Jigsaw does most things right.  The engine is solid and allows for rotation, different piece counts (max 700) and has a very usable interface.  It could be improved with a simple hotkey to bring up the preview window and while I get that it isn't the point of the engine, it would be [b]fantastic[/b] if you could import your own images.  Since you can't do that, however, the prize still goes to Jigsaw Mania (off-Steam product), but Moe Puzzle provides you with enough artwork to work from.

The arguable downsides are entirely about the content, however.  This is nothing against moe girls or anime, but rather that since they are cartoons, there is a [i]lot[/i] of negative space and same-color pieces everywhere.  Anime pin-ups lack the details that make puzzles an interesting brain exercise of breaking down an image into micro pieces.  Instead, 80% of your puzzle is "skin-tone" or flat colors and zero detail, meaning the last strokes of each puzzle in this game are simply taking the pieces you could not have possibly placed and testing them in the remaining spots.  You cannot discern one fleshy bit from another fleshy bit and even the backgrounds are pretty flat as well.  That said, if that sounds like the right kind of challenge for you, have at it.  It took me around two and a half hours to place the last 30 or so pieces of my first puzzle simply because it was all flat or slightly-shaded skin tone.

Still, it's better than assembling pictures of horses or burnt-out barns or what have you.

I like to think I'm pretty good at Survival Games. I understand the basic mechanics of the genre, and I can usually rationalize the most possible way to keep myself alive for as long as possible. However this game completely crushed that thought. The Long Dark is hardcore, punishing, screw you difficulty pumped up to mother flipping 11.

If you're first experience is the Survival Mode, you'll be dropped into a randomn spot on whatever map you chose with a varying amount of gear and clothing, depending on what difficulty you chose. And that's it. Now it's up to you to take what you have, figure out where the nearest shelter is, learn the crafting system, learn how to make a fire, learn weight management, learn to keep an eye on the sun, (or moon) learn how to evade wolfs and bears, learn the limits of your character's body temperature, rationalize which pieces of clothing would be best for your next approaching goal, figure out how to get food if you don't have a firearm, learn how to lure wolves to bears, the list just goes on and on and on and on.

There is sooooo much to keep track of in this game all at the same time, I've had to take breaks from my head hurting so bad from thinking so hard so often for so long. And the best part is: When you finally die, when a bear mauls you to death, or you freeze in the middle of a blizzard, or you fall off that rickety bridge, that's it. When you die in The Long Dark, that's all there is to it. You die, you die. No respawns, no save loads. Which makes the want to survive that much more prevalent, and real.

I would recommend this game to ANYBODY. I can't think of a single reason somebody shouldn't play this game. Even if you don't like the Survival genre, TRY IT. Wait for a sale if you have to, just try this game once! Do it!

Seeing the crusade as his holy duty, Kirk summoned up his levies and joined the armies of the Franks, Lotharingians and Italians with his, passing the Pyrenees to fulfill their holy duty to the Lord.

Oh, children, if only they knew what they had found in Tulaytulah.

By the time the war had ended three years later, Kirk's ten thousand man army of crusaders had been reduced to a tiny fraction of a broken two thousand, the rest having been killed in the Siege and subsequent Relief of Tulaytulah, along with the battles on the way to the heathen Umayyad capital. Many had thought that the Lord had forsaken them, and maybe He did, for the injuries the men had suffered as they crossed the Pyrenees once again in defeat claimed more lives than the ones they had lost in the Saracen's land. For Normandy, this was a shaming defeat.

For Jazper, however, it was nothing more than a golden opportunity.

Almost as soon as the armies of the Blessed King crossed the mountains into West Francia, his brother summoned the banners of his godless allies and marched to Melun, taking the castle in a four day long siege and overwhelming the meager garrison. This surprise move had earned the fury of Kirk, but he could do nothing but gather up mercenaries and call his allies as he made the slow, grueling march up the land of the Franks. By the time the troops had made it to southern Normandy, they had four thousand in mercenaries to add to the two thousand veteran crusaders, as well as the one thousand Italian men that managed to survive the Saracen blades. This army, however, paled in comparison to Jazper's twelve thousand men, who were now marching south after news of Kirk's arrival came to the treacherous "rightful" king of Normandy.

The next seven months were made of bloody sieges and skirmishes, as Normans fought Normans, brother fought brother, and king fought "king". In the twilight years of the conflict, the final, decisive Battle of Bourges shattered Kirk's army, with the former king now delivered to the dungeon of his disgusting, treasonous brother. With all opposition now destroyed, Jazper crowned himself King of Normandy, as well as King of England. Kirk was relegated to being the tiny Duke of Poitou, deep in the dungeons of Paris.

It seemed like the end, doesn't it, children? An unfitting end for a valiant and zealous king. But there is still more to this story, so listen closely.

Four years after the Battle of Bourges, King Jazper, now dubbed "The Monster", was bored. His latest batch of criminals to be tortured had been freed by their bandit kin, and he was disappointed that the mayor had not been successful in taking them back. While the mayor's torture had been sweet, Jazper was now deprived of a man to "practice" on. Then, he had a spectacular idea.

Jazper commanded his men to bring up his brother as he prepared a tubful of tar and a large bag of feathers,  giving the order to also prepare a wooden platform in the center of Paris. By the time all was prepared, Jazper declared that his brother, after having his army destroyed by his forces in Bourges, must now have his punishment. Suddenly, in front of the entire crowd, Jazper covered his brother in tar and ordered his men to throw feathers at him.

While I had not been present for that fateful day, legend has it that Kirk stayed proud and unbroken during the public torture, staying brave in the face of near-universal humiliation. When the King and his men had their fun, they turned to look at the crowd, which they expected to be jeering and booing.

Instead, the King was met with a flat silence. Then, slowly, a murmur began to rise up within the crowd, as they shouted for the former King Kirk to be released from his bonds. The crowd surrounded the platform, nearing the King with pitchforks, stones, dung and rotten fruits. The King's men, numbering few, tried in vain to keep the crowd back, and resorted to getting the King out.

By the end of the day, Kirk was freed by the people, and allowed by Jazper to return to his estate in Melun.

This was the start of the bloody rivalry between the Jazperite De Urduja branch and the main Parisian De Urduja branch, as Kirk, upon his return to Melun, summoned up his banners to take back his throne.

The Italians, the old allies of Kirk, immediately rushed to the banners of the rightful King, lending their three thousand to the eight thousand army. Loyalists, both noble and peasant, began coming out from the underground to give their swords to the cause of the Blessed King. Dukes from all over the kingdom, discontent with the rule of Jazper, flocked to join the King. By the time the armies had been formed and the banners went marching, the Parisian De Urdujas numbered fourteen thousand to Jazper's thirteen thousand. Normandy, as it was years earlier, went to war once again.

Both armies clashed in Bourges, Poitiers, and Paris, as the Parisians were driven back by the Jazperites as they headed for the Jazperite capital of Bordeaux. Finally, after numerous defeats and sieges, the Parisians managed to break through the Jazperite army at Lusignan, finally opening the way for the armies of Kirk to break the will of the Jazperites and reclaim the old kingdom.

However, Jazper had one more trick up his sleeve.

Just as the Parisians were beginning to set up camp outside Bordeaux, three thousand horsemen, the famously plate-clad Knights of Bordeaux, crashed into the Parisian lines as they caught the attackers off guard with a rear charge. The casualties for both sides were enormous as the infantry began trapping in the cavalry as well as repelling the garrison who had sallied out to support the charge. Initially, the Parisians were successful, as the garrison was driven back to the open gates. However, the tide of battle began to change as soon as the garrison summoned their archers and fired at the attackers below.

It was said that every arrow in that first volley hit a Parisian man, and one fateful arrow managed to pierce the helmet of the Blessed King, killing him instantly as Jazperites began surrounding his body and crushing it under their feet. The death of the King proved decisive for the battle, routing the army in the biggest mass retreat in history. The war was over, and the kingdom of Jazper was safe once more.

It's the last chapter, isn't it, children?

No.

For Kenshin, son of Kirk, and rightful King of Normandy, it isn't.

[h1]What is Kerbal Space Program[/h1]
Kerbal Space Program (or ksp) is a space and exploration simulator that does a great job at truly inspiring the idea of limitless freedom and movement in a vast solar system that mimics our own. Rather than people Squad decided to opt for a more inviting and arcade species known as kerbals. Now just because the kerbals give it an arcade look to it does not make this any less of perfection. As a simulator it can be lacking (although this can be fixed) but for any casual user looking for a game that will open their mind to our solar system this can be truly amazing and at times overwhelming due to all of the systems you have to know.

[h1]For the casual player[/h1]
For people who are looking for a fun game to maybe teach their kids or satisfy some of their own interests, this game is perfect for you. Wether you want to build rockets or airplanes or want to have a budget or contracts you can adjust all of it. The kerbals themselves are a focal point of the game and are perfect for any kids that want to play the game. With kerbals like Jebediah and Valentina leading the frontier and all of the kerbals having their own personalities it can be really fun!

[h1]For the person looking for a simulator[/h1]
If you are looking for a hyper realistic simulator of space travel then this game is not how do I say [i]complete[/i]. Lucky for you this game has one of the best modding communities I have ever seen. with nearly 1000 mods you can be sure that whatever your looking for most likely exists. Now for me the 1/10th scale earth (called kerbin) wasnt really what I was looking for. [u]Realism Overhaul[/u] was perfect for me as it solved all of my issues. If you are not familiar with realism overhaul it basically turns ksp into the most realistic space simulator on the market. Before realism overhaul getting to the moon was pretty simple and only required a bit of time effort and knowledge. But after realism overhaul just getting into a decent orbit can be extremely difficult if you dont know what your doing I highly recommend looking into it if your interested.

[h1]Final thoughts[/h1]
No matter who you are doesnt matter any kind of person can like this game and with the recent release of 1.1 and the game becoming 64 bit I can mod this game till IT CRASHES! Some terms you may want to learn include ISP, Deltav, TWR(thrust to weight), apoapsis, periapsis, and just about all the different kinds of fuel ie kerosine liquid hydrogen liquid oxygen. Happy flying!

CS:GO is in my honest opinion the greatest ever competitive shooter, I might be a bit biased with my ~1.4k h but it just has a flawless balance between individual skill (both aim and strategy) and teamwork. Most weapons have at least some use, while some may have more limited use (e.g. the negev) it feels like you see the majority of weapons at least at some point in the game, even at a pro level when watching majors. The majority of maps in this game have roots going way back and they have been perfected over multiple years and they all have their own feel, both visually and layout wise. The ranking system may not be perfect but honestly I find that it's good enough most of the time, especially with the addition of trust factor which has really improved the MM experience at least for me personally.

The game obviously has its flaws though, there are quite a bit of hackers, I have luckily never met an obvious rage hacker in my ~1k competitive matches but I'm sure there have been multiple people with more sneaky hacks such as WH. The community also isn't the greatest, don't get me wrong I've met tons of great people in this game but I've also met a ton of people that are just awful to play with, and if you want to enjoy this game to the fullest you really do need friends to play  with in my opinion. Valve also aren't the fastest at releasing updates, most of the time the updates are good and balanced (with a few exceptions such as the initial R8 and a few smoke bugs that have happened) but there really could be more of them, it being such a big game it really feels like they could have more people working on it.

Surprised I didn't hear more about this game when it came out. Admittedly, it's a very blatant Left 4 Dead clone in terms of basic mechanics. The UI is the same, most controls are the same, the formula of missions is (mostly) the same, etc.. Missions are even played with 4 characters despite there being 5 characters in the game. But this game also brings a decent amount to the table on top of everything L4D2 does; it's the same plus extra. 

Unlike L4D2, the characters aren't all played the same way, thanks to different stats and weapon rosters. Weapon traits can get pretty powerful with exotic weapons and high success chances, and coupled with the immensely powerful trinkets, add a lot of new team role functionality. There's a loot system that rewards players for completing side-objectives during missions and playing at high difficulties, as well as two crafting stations for improving or customizing your loot. Weapons and trinkets are always with your character, so you don't have to pray to get a SCAR or that silly hipfire-encouraging hunting rifle during a mission. Of course, probably the biggest change is the setting, which to me, a guy who gets a stiffy for medieval germanic aesthetic, is much better, although that's a matter of taste and others may disagree.

Probably the biggest problem I have with the game is the poor optimization. Other reviews probably mention the potential for CTDs at various points without a clear fix; this is definitely a serious problem, although it seems to only affect some people based on their rig. Also, the graphics are handled in odd ways, according to other reviews I've read, which seems to explain why lower settings are more taxing for some people than higher settings (Something to do with CPU vs. GPU usage, supposedly). For a game that's been out already for years and has even recieved new DLC recently, these kinds of problems suggest the developers are, at best, unprofessional, and at worst, totally uninterested in assuring their paid-for work is up to par.

It also lacks some longevity outside of farming that would make it a highly-played part of my library. Probably the only thing this game neglected to copy from L4D2 is Versus mode, for some reason, which is an unfortunate thing to neglect, and I don't understand why it was. Maybe they tried and the special rats weren't balanced when played by humans, but they don't seem so different from special infected in L4D2.

It's a good game and can serve as a superior alternative to L4D2, but it costs too much considering it isn't entirely stable and only offers a bit of original content, especially when L4D2 was given out for free a few years ago. If a Versus mode was added and the game was more stable, I'd consider the current price at least close to reasonable, but until that happens, this is a sale-only purchase. But goddamn, what a worthy purchase when it is on sale.

Firstly, I'd recommend it for fans of hack & slash gameplay. However, it has several issues with the PC port. It's got a hard time with widescreen monitors. The resolution scaling is totally off! Setting it to fullscreen actually shrinks the game's screen and distorts the text, as if stretching a lower resolution. I needed a MOD to get it to run in proper fullscreen. Using that mod, I don't have a mouse cursor in the game... at all. Using the windowed mode doesn't let me adjust the size of the window, so I can only see about 1/3 of the game. The keybindings can be awkward since this game was designed for the PS4. There is no dodge button, nor can you bind it to a key. If I equip the taunt module for 2B and 9S, I can't use it using a keyboard. The "flight" sections of the game are awkward with a mouse and keyboard. If you play for long periods, it will begin to stutter more often, at least for my rig. I've had about 7 crashes so far. Most, if not all, crashes were due to using the steam overlay or alt-tabbing. Other than that, it runs mostly well. Though, with an i7 4790k, 16Gb of DDR3 RAM, about 4 TB of storage, and a GTX 980ti, I really should not be dropping FPS with this game's graphical fidelity.

Onto subjective things: The melee combat, music, and story are all well done! The "flight" sections of the game are basically galaga sections or similar types of games. Combining that with the epic music and an epic setting TOTALLY destroyed my immersion. It's like putting nerf guns into the fight scenes of serious war movies. I would have liked them to do what games like Black Ops 3 did with their flight sections. They were simplified because the main focus is obviously infantry combat, but it did not destroy my immersion. I wasn't going to expect Ace Combat, nor should anyone. The big slow-moving jpeg bubbles of damage definitely didn't help with the immersion either. Sure, fire enough and it'll get very difficult to avoid being hit, but geez how did humanity lose to an army that uses bubble-blowers as their primary ranged weapon? Not to mention they can be destroyed by shooting them with bullets or smacking them with melee weapons. The machines are derpy-looking except for the bosses (thankfully). I do appreciate the effort that went into the story as well as the easter-egg types of endings and nostalgia-like gameplay segments, like with the hacking minigame (except for the "flight" sections). It makes sense why 9S is a young boy. (It's a stereotype) The graphics are... pretty bad. I wasn't going to expect Crysis or Battlefield, but geeeeeez they make half-life 2 look like a graphical masterpiece in 2017. The animations are thankfully well done, except for lip-syncing. 

It may sound like I expect too much from games, but this is a $60 release. It has to compare to other $60 games. It comes up short in too many areas to justify recommending it at its current price. This is a $50 game at maximum! $45 would be good. It's like selling a beat-up used car with a good sound system at the same price as a brand new car of the same model. If The Witcher 3's devs could do it, so could these devs. Now THAT is a game deserving of the $60 price!

Good game.

Graphics: Pixel graphics. Done really well, but does not have any breathless moments. Just a standard level of goodness (whatever that would be.) Other games have definitely done it better, but this game isn't something to laugh at. However, while the sprites look perfectly fine and good, some of the portraits could arguably be done better. A few of them look a bit strange, but it won't really be a huge problem.

Gameplay: Moving to the rhythm and fighting to the rhythm will be really hard the first few hours of the game. However, you can feel yourself get better as you can keep trying and trying. You can buy permanent upgrades for playing each individual Zone. There are Zones 1 through 4 (No DLC) and Zones 1 through 5 (DLC). Those upgrades only apply to that. Other than that, there are different modes to play like "All Zones Mode" where you have to play all 4 or 5 zones without dying. All upgrades unlocked, lower health. There's a lot more so check the wiki, this review is already getting long. Also check for each character difference. Every character is different. Also there's digging. Dirt, stone, stone brick, gold brick, bedrock. Different levels of shovels are needed. Base only digs dirt. Hitting stone with base shovel removes coin multiplier. This section is already long, there's a lot to take note of, okay?

Music: It's good and catchy, as expected from a game based around music and beats. It is somewhat hard to hear the beats for some songs, but you will get used to it. There are several different versions of the soundtrack that you can select, from the original DannyB to FamilyJules (Metal). Each Zone has a different style of music, like electro to rock. I don't know the order and what each song genre each zone is so you can look that up too.

Sound: The grunts of slashing and the sounds of each miniboss and attacks are VERY distinctive. The grunts that your character makes while fighting help to keep to the beat, and the steps and sounds of the minibosses help you react to it a little better. Example, Dragons make huge steps, while a Nightmare makes a distinctly different sound +the visual queue of darkness. The encounter with them also makes different sounds like screaming, bellowing, etc.

tl;dr: game is great with decent graphics and very distinctive. it's hard but rewarding. I probably missed something in regards to how much you can talk about in terms of modes and mechanics.

I'll start this off by stating while this review is POSITIVE I don't recommend buying it right now, unless you really want to just screw around.

tl;dr: The game is fun, has a good solid foundation of enjoyable mechanics to build off of, but currently does not have enough things to do with said mechanics.

So the bad things, as of this review, which is Early Access and very likely to change later on I imagine:
-Beetles
-Physics are wonky as hell sometimes (randomly jettisoned off of your ship or into a wall and die instantly)
-Fall damage is overly punishing (healing items are plentiful, even early on, but it's still annoying losing a quarter/half of your health because of small falls)
-islands often not having enough interesting things on them (though whether this is because spawn coding isn't placing lootables properly or just the islands I've visited haven't had spots set properly by their creators, I don't know)
-Beetles
-FUCKING
-BEETLES
-A general lack of things to do currently beyond build fancy ship and explore, there's pvp but encountering people once you get past early zones is relatively rare
-almost requires a group to play effectively, not just from a "fun" perspective, as a functional defensible ship requires multiple positions manned
-A general lack of direction early on (likely to be fixed by a tutorial or some similar thing later on)
-Seriously, fuck beetles

And now onto the GOOD things:
-Grapple mechanic is one of the most enjoyable physic based movement systems I've ever touched
-Highly customizable airships, can make anything from a tub to a flying tower
-Player created islands tend to have really impressive designs
-Most players are non-hostile (only a good thing if you're mostly wanting a fun ship building exploration game)
-cosmetics are rare enough to be exciting when you get one, but not so rare you never get anything new
-A VERY solid basis for exciting gameplay mechanics later on
-You can kill the beetles
-No really you just shoot them
-You can grapple the beetles to be taken on a magical journey
-A notable lack of dog enemies
-Sky pirates and shiet

Obviously my bad points are bit more fleshed out at the moment, but as it is literally the first early access release I'd like to believe a good amount of those will change, it's still a solid game to have fun with even now, just don't expect lasting power unless you're the kind of person who likes being an absolute sky pirate with your buddies and just blasting everyone you see.

Anyways if you read my rambling this far, you may have some mental deficiency quite frankly, but kudos anyways.

I was really excited to try Arma 3, and I really tried to like it. The single player is decent, the gameplay is great, everything looks beautiful and sounds awesome.

Why am I not recommending this?

The multiplayer.

If you don't want to be in a server with 400+ ping, or that is empty, you'd better love being in a sims-esque server where only whitelisted people can pick up things, and claim it is 'RP'ing as a criminal' to shoot you for no reason.

Servers that function as actual combat game modes are great, except it costs in-game currency to use vehicles and new weapons (earned through getting kills), and you spawn quite far from anything. Added to that is the frustration of being shot in the back by teammates, or run over by them any time you get close to the action. Also, you need to level up to use different weapons (which you have to buy once you unlock them) but you earn XP at such a low rate compared to the amount it takes to level, it's just not worth the trouble. I can see it being fun if the servers weren't mostly all RP servers that don't allow you to do anything unless you become whitelisted, or the community was a little less trigger happy towards anyone they do not know personally, regardless of the team.

It has amazing potential, but the multiplayer is awful, and that was pretty much the selling point for me. If you enjoy singleplayer tactical hyperrealistic shooters, you will love it. If you're getting it for the multiplayer, you'd better either be ready to apply for a whitelist for the worst RP servers I have ever encountered (childishly immature, seems completely unmoderated), or be ready to be teamkilled every time you leave your spawn zone. Most servers have extremely high ping, meaning the large selection of servers isn't too large when you eliminate 80% that are unplayably laggy and most of the rest are empty.

The game initially comes off like a lot of effort has been put into it (which I don't totally doubt). There are sweet mini-games, the dad is pretty customizable, there is an option for binder-dads (for dads who bind), you get to meet the dads in a manner that makes sense, and you get to make a choice in the game where it's basically one dad or the other. However, after that point, there's no juggling of schedules or dads which could, for one, make a specific playthrough more interesting (though the writing is more complicated, I'm sure more people would be tempted to buy the game just for their own exploration purposes if the game was more convoluted) and the writing more complicated and interesting since the story would be forced to develop in many interesting and specific ways. I find the depth of the game really lacks partially as a result of that. Amanda is really the only other aspect you need to juggle, but the game never gets to a point where you need to choose between Amanda's well-being and a love interest or....yourself. So, in reality, Amanda is a piece of cake to handle (she really is a great kid though) and you're not ever really juggling anything. There's not much challenge to the game besides the mini-games and being careful in your responses. Each dad route feels like it could take that next step and that the point you reach at the end of each one feels like it's the beginning of the relationship....maybe even barely? There are both good endings and bad endings in this game, but the game ultimately really only has one ending that changes slightly depending on your relationship with the dads and I guess also depending on your relationship with Amanda. It's a little disappointing in its end game and I really thought this game was going to expand out into having a part 2 after the 3 dates (as in the story really only progresses so far until you do the 3 dates). Another thing that this game lacked was, imo, significant milestones. Don't get me wrong, there's really memorable parts that are really well written and super funny (significant pro of this game: the dialogue), but I feel like there are parts that could be even more special if we had milestone art or something thrown in there. I appreciate the dad relationships and the platonic love that progresses pretty well into romantic love, but I would have loved more romance, more intimate interaction, etc. Compared to other dating games, this did better in some ways like with the mini-games. I would say the writing was better and I really want to, but I feel like I was held out on. I definitely feel like there should have been more and I am a little disappointed because I wanted to love the game so much, but having been familiar with other dating sims and even just games that weave a romantic aspect into them, my expectations were higher.

If you're looking for a game that gets the adrenaline pumping and is full of exhilarating moments, then this is definitely one of those games! It's extremely fun and gets you hooked once you start to get the hang of it, but first lets get to what I like about the game.

-The audio is spectacular and is really satisfying. Landing a head shot or tearing through hordes of enemies with a huge axe, is just really satisfying to listen to and adds unto the game play. Now I'm not one for hard rock or metal music, but it goes very well with the game and complements the brutal, gory, and fun nature of the game.

-The game play is very fun and gets addictive. There's a wide variety of ways to play differing between 10 classes with their own type of weapons and sets of abilities. Whatever class you prefer, you'll get different experiences such as melting enemies with flame throwers, decapitating them with a sword, blowing up things to hell, or just sniping heads off one by one, with a multitude of fun ways to play the game, you won't be bored for a while. I also have to mention, that the animations of the weapons are crisp and amazing, especially with melee weapons and how different attacks register with the hitbox. It may seem like this game is simply just shooting things and bashing heads in, but it's much more complex than that, such as using different attacks like thrusting a sword to land headshots, parrying incoming attacks, or stunning tanky enemies with grenades to better take them out. Game play is just pure fun and does take some knowledge and some tactics if you want to become better at it and tackle higher difficulties. I almost forgot to mention, there's also slow motion that makes you feel more like a badass.

-There's custom maps and community servers which even adds more gameplay aspects and fun to the game.

-Customizations like headgear, gun skins, and things like that are pretty cool looking. With enough time and effort, you can get some awesome looking skins and gear. 

Now to my dislikes

-Like how I mentioned before, the customizations are cool and awesome, but it's entirely based on a rng loot box system. Now there's loot boxes called vosh vault crates that you can only earn through playing the game and has some nice and decent looking customizations, though the really cool customizations, you have to buy using keys or buying the item at the marketplace. Basically it's like CS GO's loot system, except better because at least there's some customizations you can unlock through time and effort.

-Now it may depend on your specs, but I've experienced a number of crashes, especially frozen screens that forced me to reset my PC and kills my mood to even continue. Though at least it's not a common occurrence that makes the game unplayable but It is still very annoying and took me some time to get used to.

-The matchmaking is WHACK, there's no peer to peer and only dedicated servers you can join. If there's a specific map you want or gamemode or you're playing with a group of friends, you cannot simply create a match, but instead find a dedicated server with those filters you've applied, sometimes there is no server with what you want or it may just take a long time to find one. 

Overall, the game is incredible and is extremely fun once you really start to get the hang of it. The gameplay, animations, and sound design are superb and satisfying, especially with a lot things going on such as explosions, decapitations, and flying corpses. Then there are some downsides like the bad matchmaking, the limitations of customizations and the crashes, Though the gameplay overcomes all of the negatives and makes it all the worth while.

This game is really damn good. And that was unexpected, to me, after all, who expects anything from a Wolfenstein, especially after Wolf 2009? As a sequel-reboot, this game is all parts visceral, gritty, and smart.
The story is simple, of course- what if the Nazis had won WW2 with a little help from some ancient technology so advanced as to seem supernatural? That's the game's only hook into its mystic past. That's where the simplicity ends- the story is brilliant and brutal, told initially through the eyes of BJ, an invalid, forced to watch from his wheelchair as the Nazis take over the world, systematically killing everyone they deem untermensch. It's enough to give you great catharsis when he finally stands up from his chair. The characters are superbly animated and acted, giving real life to the world. BJ is actually cast as something of the typical action hero, optimistic and unsuited for the gritty world he finds himself in, it works.
The gameplay is pretty standard FPS faire. It's got enough enemies for BJ to mow down to harken back to earlier Wolf, you can even wield akimbo weapons owing to BJ being a meathead. Enemy variety is good and the level design is impressive, often monolithic Nazi architecture though there are several excursions to unique locations- concentration camps, U-boats, the Nazi moonbase, etc. It's even got a decent length for a singleplayer FPS these days, about 20 hours.

When I first saw this game in the store I thought it looked like an uninspired ARPG school project.
After having played it for 30 hours I am happy to admit that my early and superficial judgement was 100% wrong.

The thing I am most baffled by is how in the world I managed to enjoy the shit out of an unfinished game with no story, uninspired graphics, no relatable characters and an uninteresting world. 

The key here is how well Chronicon puts together its mechanics. It feels good to play, and has enough going on mechanically to make it fun for hours on end. 

There is a real depth and complexity to every build, and you can tailor every item to your liking through an incredibly flexible enchanting system. The hunger for loot and xp, which drives any good ARPG, is present here, and it feels damn good to get new gear and skills to play around with all the way till lvl 100. 

Don't expect to dedicate your life to it, though. At around 30 hours I am spent and probably won't be playing much more of it. It's rare to find an ARPG I feel satisfied quitting, but this is one of them. I got more than my money's worth, and if more content gets added, maybe i'll check in again. (like, add online multiplayer and i'll buy it for all my friends)

I like this game a lot, and would recommend it to anyone slightly intrigued by it.

So after seeing the amount of recent negative reviews from people that haven't even played the game properly and I mean putting like 30 minutes to 2 hours into it I wanted to make my own review.

So firstly I'll state that a CONTROLLER is necessary as the mouse/keyboard controls are bad unless you can adept to it, I know I didn't. 

I'm not going to talk about the game other than my opinion as there are plenty of reviews from others that talk about the game. 

Story:
The Story wasn't too bad for me, I enjoyed it except for when Livie comes in as I found her to be quite annoying but otherwise I enoyed it. 

Map:
With the maps it was sad how they never varied, as in go to a snow area and the map will be chosen out of a selection of 6 snow maps for example, so they just don't stand out or are just meh to look at.

Controls:
The controls are solid except for aiming as it easily gets out of line when the creatures fight around high/low terrain or jump around so you'll eventually not be able to hit properly with the assault rifle unless you use homing shots. Aside from that I myself like to keep the ground in my sight so at least if water is in front of me, rather than running into it like a wall I can just run around it instantly, not exactly a big issue but it was another problem I had during melee.

Gameplay:
Gameplay was mostly ok except for 1 thing and that's how bad RNG is on this and I mean bad. I've spent hours playing the same mission for 1 drop from a certain creature just to do a single upgrade. Collecting the skill upgrades to throw on your weapon/gun/shield was rediculous as again it was RNG based and bad at that, even when combining them to get a high grade one it was a very tiny chance of getting the one you want...

Aside from bad RNG the fights were fun and once you got into the high levels they get really intense but interesting too. You'd start having to think more than normal and do a little bit of planning as you would easily get grouped on by a number of creatures which would normally give you a ton of problems/deaths if unlucky. 

The AI aren't that good but can be a bit ok. I tend to use Nana, Lindow and Gilbert on most of my missions as unlike the rest they barely let me down, aside from the missions that I know they'd be useless on.

Rageburst/Blood Arts:
Blood Arts are fun as they can give you a unique attack however there is a lot of them to check out so it's worth playing around with them. Rageburst mode is nice but trying to get the requirements met for max damage output can be headache, if selecting a few like 15 hits, 10k damage and 1 devour it's easy to obtain but you'll only get like say %250 damage increase, if you select every requirement and do it you can get say %500 damage increase but that's assuming you meet all those requirements otherwise you need to start the rage mode and requirements all over again.

Multiplayer:
Haven't tried and as much as people say it's broken or doesn't work well there are a few guides you can check out to give it a shot if you're up for it.

Can't think of anything else worth noting so I'll leave this as is, not a great review but hopefully it gives some insight and a bit of a heads up with what to expect from the game.

I had "Bear With Me" on my wishlist for a good while, and when it went on sale, I finally decided to buy the game.  

It started out as an interesting game about a kid, Amber, and her stuffed bear, Ted, a detective, trying to find Amber's missing brother, Flint.  While the premise might sound childish, this game is in no way a children's game.  Things start to get dark: the "Red Man" is bringing destruction to Paper City, home of Amber's stuffed animal friends, and Amber's search for Flint occasionally brings up brief Lynch-like visions (strange messages on walls, giant eyes, etc.).  Still, despite the dark elements, Amber and Ted's interactions with each other keep things from being too dark.

This changes a bit in the second episode, when things take a definite turn for the darker, with elements of corruption and behind the scenes manipulation being brought in.  Paper City is rather gritty for a child's imaginary city: a corrupt mayor, a mob boss casino owner, a mentally unstable superhero, and an increasing amount of destruction and presence of the "Red Man."  The second episode ends on a bit of both a tearjerker and a cliffhanger.

The third episode.  Wow.  This episode was the darkest of the three installments.  The familiar humor was still there, but the darker and sadder moments were far more numerous.  Loose ends get tied up, with the "Red Man's" identity revealed, as well as finally showing where Flint is.  There were more puzzles in this episode as well.  (The vault one was especially tricky.  I ended up brute-forcing it my first time through.)  The game has two endings; both of them are quite sad.

The controls were easy to figure out-- the standard "point, click, drag" format used in other games of this type.

The dialogue made me laugh out loud several times.  The overall idea of a teddy bear as a hardboiled detective is a pretty interesting one, but it worked.  Ted and Amber's relationship really made the game interesting, especially when they have flashbacks about how they met.  There are also a lot of great references and shoutouts (such as, but not limited to: the Necronomicon, Silent Hill, The Big Lebowski, IT, The Exorcist, H.P. Lovecraft, Batman, and The Wizard of Oz).

I liked the noir look to the game and definitely got a kick out of being rewarded for thoroughly examining every item.  (And if nothing else, the comments that the characters make are great, especially when they break the fourth wall.)

My one issue with the game is the overall length; I was able to complete a full playthrough of the first installment in one sitting (92 minutes), and that was with backtracking and watching cutscenes.  Episode two, likewise, was a bit on the short side; it did have more choices involved, as well as more exploration.  Episode three is quite long, although the puzzles help pad it out quite a bit.  

Overall, it was a very enjoyable series.  I laughed, I cried, and at the end, I felt like the story had been told well.  I would love to see more games from this team!

***The first three sentences were my original review from over a year ago. The rest is a take after returning from a very long hiatus***

The atmosphere is brutal, and unforgiving.

The devs are very communicative with the players.

Mainly posting this review to mitigate some of the people crying about optimization.

********************What now?********************

Having returned after over a year of not playing I can deftly say that my original thoughts on this game hold true; this game is brutal, and unforgiving. However, the good has stayed, the bad has left.

Whether playing solo, or with a partner, you'll want to be on your toes for every second. Be ready for some cheap shots you might not agree with and, some wins that will scratch an itch like no other

Not to sound cliche' but, Hunt: Showdown is the epitome of Dark Souls battle royale. The only difference is the theme. You're going to die... A lot... You're going to scoff constantly. You're going to get angrier than you thought you would- or, should- at a video game. You're going to hate it.

Then, you're going to win.

You're going to appreciate the skulking, the planning, the necessary communication (though, you should keep it to a minimum), and the trust you need to develop with yourself, or a teammate. This game isn't about speed; it's about a REAL hunt. Stay low, move slow, and always be checking your six.

To the original complaints about optimization: don't expect to be able to play it on mom's laptop in her den, and don't think your $400 PC you built 3 years ago will be able to coast along on medium settings. It's still a horse. Albeit a smooth-running horse, now.

The sound design is the best I've ever heard. Period. It is the most immersive (and necessary) element of this game. It is key to every decision you make while hunting. You WILL need to know what's going on around you at all times, and a halfway decent pair of headphones will really give you a leg up on your opponents, whether they be human or AI.

I can't recommend this game enough. You don't need to be a dead-shot but, you do need to have some wits, and common sense. This isn't a twitch shooter. You will die with one well-placed headshot, even from one of the weaker rifles. This is about hunting while being hunted at the same time.

Do not get overconfident. You will get taken down many pegs if you think you're going to be playing PUBG, or Fortnite. This is a very calculated, and cold game. Be aware of your surroundings as much as you can. Learn what risks are, and are not, worth taking. Once you've left a game with one, or BOTH bounties, you'll get it. The name "Hunt: Showdown" isn't a misnomer. You need to treat it like a real hunt. That's all there is to it.

About two weeks ago I was lamenting how few space games actually allow for zero-g movement, usually they are set in locations that while technically in space, have some sort of artificial gravity. Then along comes Tacoma and what do you know, it's got some sweet zero-g movement. Nice!

Tacoma is a (quote unquote) walking-simulator story game by Fullbright, the studio behind the somewhat polarizing Gone Home (in my library but have not played yet - shame on me). I dislike the term walking-simulator, not because it's wrong - lets face it you walk around a lot in most first person games, but because it's not really what you spend most of your time doing. Tacoma is a "pick things up look at them and-put them back simulator". 

I don't mean that in a bad way either, the level of detail that goes into every object and the environments of Tacoma is ridiculous. Each item you can pick up is made to look and seem as real (in the game world) as possible. And it's not for nothing, these items make up the world, give you details and flesh out the time and place you are in. They add gravitas, humor and more. Yes you can blow through Tacoma without picking up a single object, but why? Stop look and smell (well pick up and closely inspect) the flowers.

That's not to say that's all there is to Tacoma, the core of Tacoma is the story it tells and in order to not accidentally spoil anything I will be brief. You take on the role of Amy Ferrier, who has been tasked with investigating the events of what happened on the Tacoma space station and retrieve the on board AI named ODIN. Exploration and interaction will reveal the events of the last few weeks/days/hours leading up to the current situation. Throughout the game you become familiar with the small crew of diverse and real-feeling people that make up Tacoma's staff.

The primary game mechanic is to watch pre-recorded sequences of conversations via an enhanced reality interface. You will see and hear the crew walk around the locations of the ship in these sequences and be able to scrub back and forth through these recordings as people come and go. Sometimes you will follow a person or conversations out of the room, only to have to scrub back and watch from a different angle to see another part. It's quite brilliant and the format is something that really only works in video games. I honestly hope it's something that gets used again in other games.

There were a few things that bothered me such as not being able to see your feet/legs except in particular pre-set circumstances and how some of the interactions limit you for story reasons, nothing game breaking. Really I just wanted more - more recordings, more interactions, more story background (more zero-g!). I was compelled by what they gave me and much like last weeks review of Signal From Tölva, we only get the tip of the iceberg, and I want to sink my ship on the whole thing.

Interacting with these recordings and peaking into the lives of the crew has a slightly voyeuristic feel to it that at first I wasn't sure about. Not in an uncomfortable way, just more along the lines of wondering, is this really necessary? But your character is really just a neutral observer and it's far more about what you put into it, your interest level as the player. You can complete Tacoma by doing almost nothing but standing around and waiting, but the design and detail of the station invites you to investigate. "Come take a look" Tacoma says, "I have such wonderful things to show you" (just kidding on that last one - this isn't Event Horizon). 

Tacoma isn't long and it isn't complicated but it is a fascinating piece of interactive fiction featuring a well designed mechanic that's put to great use. Take your time when going through the space station Tacoma, it's not a race and it will reward you. Play it with someone, like movie night - only with more freedom.

TLDR: Not for me.  I found it frustrating and counter intuitive.  Good simulation of someone with absolutely no survival skills suddenly finding themselves up sh*t's creek with no paddle.

----------------------------

I wanted to like this.  I really did.  But there are a few MAJOR problems right off the bat.  In Story mode, I found myself dieing over and over before I could even get to the crash site because the numbnutt player character (here after called Numbnutts) would get cold, get dizzy and walk off a cliff, causing him to die.  After the third time, it stopped being funny and really started making me wish I could make him eat toxic plants or fight a grizzly bear without weapons. 

So I tried sandbox survival.  Not much better.  It dropped me in the middle of the woods where it's 0 degrees C with plenty of supplies EXCEPT Numbnutts seems to forget that without proper winter clothing, you freeze to death in minutes.  So, here I am with Numbnutts, medical supplies, food, soda, wood, tinder, matches, etc and NO warm clothes to speak of.  By the time I found shelter (sort of...not sure a cabin that looks like it got bombed counts as shelter) where I could build a fire, I was 9/10ths dead from the cold.  So I built a fire, ate my food, drank my soda, spread out my bed roll, and put some snow on to melt.  Then Numbnutts gets dizzy from being tired so I told him to sleep for 1 hour.  Woke up, the water was evaporated and the fire was out.  F-ing great.  Numbnutts can't even prepare for the cold weather, so why would I think he could build a proper fire or melt snow?  Oh, did I mention that NONE of my "Condition" meter refilled while sleeping?  So I'm STILL 9/10ths dead and now I have NO water, NO food and NO tinder (which means no fire).  Now I have to go look for wood and...you guessed it...Numbnutts dies in the snow because he's too cold and his health bar or what ever it is ticks down to empty.  Great...there's a half an hour I would like back.  That brings me to another point.  Water obtained from melting snow should be 99% safe.  Especially if the snow is in the middle of an uninhabited wilderness.  Once you boil it, unless there is some chemical impurity (not likely if the place is uninhabited), water is 99% safe.  Now, if the snow has a red twinge to it, a.k.a. Watermelon Snow, that's another story.  Stay away from that (seriously, IRL, that can kill you if you ingest it). 

So, please, tell me, where is the fun in this?  The game opens up with a reminder that this is NOT a survival simulator and is just a game and yet, it seems to be a really good simulation of what will happen to people who have no survival training what so ever when the world ends.

As it stands, it doesn't work.  At least, not for me.  There needs to be a LOT of tweaks before I'll give this another shot.  I can't fathom a real life scenario where someone ends up in the Canadian wilderness with a can of sardines and an orange soda but  without a proper coat.  At the very least, you should have something warmer than long underwear and jeans.  And when I say "coat" I mean a real coat.  Like a down filled parka or something.  There is no excuse for gimping the player from the get go by starting him off freezing to death.  You would think that your instinct to collect wood and get a fire going would be the answer but no....it isn't.  Your condition deteriorates when you do anything if you're too cold and you eventually die trying to keep warm.

In conclusion, if you like frustrating, counter intuitive game play, knock yourself out.  If you like a game that give you almost no clear direction and punishes you (with death) for not jumping on it's logic train from square one, go for it.  Personally, I recommend getting a survival mod for Skyrim or just playing Fallout 4 (or New Vegas) on survival.  Stay away from this "Kings Quest" train of thought.  Lastly, anyone who says anything along the lines of "go read a guide" can gargle my balls.  A game should clearly present it's concepts without needing a walk through to be understood and enjoyed.  If your game needs a guide, you really need to rework your game because it's designed poorly.

More than a good game, more than a bad one, I prefer an INTERESTING game. With its dark and clever metacommentary on the Star Wars universe itself, its multilayered characters, and a truly bleak atmosphere that conveys the horrors of war far more than any weepy montage of Jedi Knights getting gunned down, Knights of the Old Republic 2 (KotOR2) more than fits the bill.

HOWEVER, IT IS VERY IMPORTANT THAT YOU DOWNLOAD SOME KIND OF CONTENT PATCH FOR THIS GAME. KotOR2 was rushed for the holidays, and a ton of vital content was left on the cuttng room floor, from characters scenes to incredibly important plot details. The Sith Lords Restoration Patch is one of the best. DO NOT play this game without something like that.

Following closely the heels of the first game, KotOR2 examines in more depth exactly what would happen to the people of a galaxy after decades of war, and it isn't pretty. From the protagonist to the party members, everyone has been scarred...and the scars are more subtle than some bomb-scorched landscape. It takes a simultaneously more mystical view of the Force and a more critical view. After all, has the Force really done anything in the Star Wars universe but perpetuate years for its thousand-year history?

Of course, the game has some clever "outs" built into the story to keep the deconstructions from getting too heavy--some unreliable narration, though you'll have to play for yourself to see what I mean. And while the game plays well enough, it's essentially more of the same KotOR we got last time...along with the same massively overpowered character you get by the end of the game. All these goes with the afformentioned fact that the game really isn't done--the pacing can be a mess towards the end, even with the patch.

Ultimately, it's up to you whether this makes the game worthwhile. As for me, this is one of my all-time favorites. It made me think--not just about Star Wars, but about the world outside of it. And I say that if a game can do that, it's damn worth a few hills of bugs.

A brutally difficult game that combines the visual aesthetics of Minecraft with the tactical combat of the original X-Com. Default difficulty (which allows achievements) comes with ironman (lack of) saves, so beware!

The plot is short and to the point: the world has been taken over by four boss characters. It’s up to you to stop them.

You start with three characters: two random allies and you, a character who, aside from determining your starting world, and having a blank slate as far as skill points (you have 5 points to assign as you choose), is totally expendable – it’s entirely possible that by the time you get to the second (or even first!) boss that your party will not include any of the original three members.

You’re thrown into combat as soon as you leave your house, and depending on which world you started on (‘platformer’ world - which has giant mushrooms, green pipes, floating treasure boxes, and red brick walls - tends to be the hardest start, with the possibility of spawning living bombs who throw themselves at you, blowing huge chunks out of the area and killing pretty much anything unfortunate enough to be in the blast radius) you may well start losing characters just about immediately.

There are a number of different weapon classes which you can use: various melee weapons, pistols, rifles, bows, crossbows, spells and staffs (which throw out small bomb-like or inferno projectiles), and perhaps my favorite: brute strength, which allows you to rip out chunks of the game world and throw them at your enemies.

And here we come to one of the more fun aspects of ENEMY – the entire world is made up of little cubes, which can (and will) be destroyed in the course of your fighting. Walls will get holes in them, and will eventually buckle; trees will fall down in an explosion of leaf blocks. Trying to get into the boss castle, but the corridor outside the throne room is a deathtrap? Blow a hole in a back wall and go through that way, or if you can make your way up to the roof, toss a bomb and crush everything in a rain of bricks!

Both sounds and music are basic, but serve well enough.

Only two things come to mind as complaints: first that the interface doesn’t seem to have any way to automatically make sure that you hold enough APs in reserve to fire a shot during your interrupt; second is that the game can start to struggle if there are large amounts of bricks falling all at once, as can very well happen in town battles if you (and/or the enemy) use lots of bombs, fire, or staff weapons.

Well worth picking up if any of the above catches your interest.

Quick, clever and risky game. Probably one of the most refreshing games in turn-based strategy.

Games are about 20-30 rounds long. You're a wizard with a card and deck mechanic where you can summon creature, or cast powerful spells to hopefully kill all of your opponents. Tricks and dirty plays are totally allowed! Risky moves are always rewarded!

Solid Rating: 9/10.

The game requires that you make smart moves and risky decisions that will lead you to the killing blow of your foe.

Cool things: no need to 'build' a deck. Your wizard's equipments will define your card pool to play for each battle.

A few things I have issues with so far: 
- 'Burning' your hand to get the mega-spell could be abused to the point of only having that spell...
- Not being able to track your opponent's mana % to his mega-spell (although relatively unecessary)
- Map editor? :P
- Could use a 'longer' or custom games.

I don't review games often, but I'll try to be very short because my feelings about this game are immense. I don't have nearly the hours that many long term players do, but this game finally got off my wishlist when it was on sale and I'm extremely glad that albeit late, I gave it a try. This game has so many levels of detail that it is staggering. The galaxy is stunning in every single aspect both in terms of size, density and accuracy to our own galaxy. The graphics are still incredible by my standards and I am extremely excited to see that the future of this game is bright with the Odyssey expansion announced. If you like exploration, decisions that are the small changes actually affecting the world around you, thrilling space combat, or just space in general, I really do recommend you play this game. It has many many routes and possibilities you can take that I believe just about any style of gamer will find enjoyable.
